The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a minuscule wet weight of just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], reflecting the modest energy reserves contained within the small, transparent egg which has a diameter of roughly 0.8 millimeters. This initial larval mass is among the lowest recorded for members of the Arripidae family, underscoring the species' reliance on a high-quality planktonic food supply immediately following the onset of exogenous feeding. The larvae, which are initially lecithotrophic, undergo a critical trophic switch as they absorb their yolk reserves and begin actively foraging on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton, a transition that typically occurs within a few days of the hatching event.

As the developing fish grow and undergo larval metamorphosis, they transition from a pelagic ichthyoplanktonic existence to a more demersal lifestyle as post-settlement juveniles. During this phase, individuals experience a period of rapid somatic growth, though the progression toward sexual maturity is relatively prolonged compared to many other coastal perciform fishes. Corresponding to this length at the onset of reproductive maturation, the wet weight at puberty is calculated to be approximately 309 grams [Wwp = approximately 309 grams], a body mass that signifies a substantial energetic investment in somatic tissue prior to any allocation toward gamete production. This size threshold is a critical life-history milestone, as it represents the point at which individuals transition from an exclusively somatic growth trajectory to one that balances continued increases in length with the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis.

The asymptotic or ultimate body size of Arripis trutta represents the maximum standard length attainable by the species under optimal environmental conditions. Extensive sampling of commercial and recreational catches, combined with age-at-length data from otolith analyses, indicates that the ultimate standard length approaches 89 centimeters [Li = 89 centimeters], a formidable size that places the Australian salmon among the larger members of the nearshore pelagic fish community in temperate Australian waters. At this maximum length, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is roughly 9,400 grams [Wwi = roughly 9,400 grams], a figure that aligns closely with the heaviest recorded individuals, which have been documented at approximately 9.4 kilograms. The relationship between length and mass in this species is well described by a power function, with the allometric exponent indicating that weight increases disproportionately faster than length, a common pattern in fishes that accumulate substantial musculature and lipid reserves as they approach their upper size limit. Attaining such a large body size requires several years of consistent feeding on energy-rich prey such as pilchards, anchovies, and squid.

The lifespan of Arripis trutta, determined through the enumeration of annual growth increments in sagittal otoliths from individuals collected across its geographic range, has been estimated at approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years] when the fish are reared under the average thermal conditions of their native habitat at 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]. This longevity is notably high for a fast-growing, pelagic-feeding species and suggests a life-history strategy that combines rapid early growth with a prolonged reproductive window. The maximum recorded lifespan implies that mature individuals may participate in multiple spawning seasons over several decades, contributing to the species' resilience against variable recruitment success. Such a long adult life stage is energetically demanding, requiring the maintenance of metabolic function and swimming performance throughout senescence. The consistent thermal environment at 17.4 °C likely plays a key role in modulating the pace of aging, as cooler temperatures are generally associated with reduced metabolic rates and extended lifespans in ectothermic vertebrates like fishes.

Reproductive output in Australian salmon is tightly linked to female body size, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the next generation through heightened fecundity. Spawning occurs in coastal waters during the austral spring and summer, where females release multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the course of the reproductive season. The size at which females first participate in spawning, the standard length at puberty of 31.5 centimeters [Lp = 31.5 centimeters], is a key parameter for fisheries management, as it defines the minimum size at which individuals should be allowed to mature before harvest. The companion metric, the wet weight at puberty of 309 grams [Wwp = 309 grams], provides an alternative descriptor of this energetic threshold. Together, these values indicate that females must accumulate a critical mass of approximately 309 grams before investing energy into egg production, a strategy that ensures sufficient somatic reserves to support the high metabolic costs of vitellogenesis and spawning migrations.
